--- title: "Audit experiments" subtitle: "Extended course – day 3" format: revealjs # Optional runs that this deck includes in its main flow (core-runs.lua # strips their .deepdive mark); the others stay on the d toggle. This deck # has no optional runs. core-runs: [] --- ## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.todaymeta} Session 1 of day 3, on the design of the housing audit ::: :::: {.todaybox} ::: {.nonincremental .fs-85} 1. Random assignment – what it guarantees, balance, and names as treatments 2. Analysis – the comparison among replies, and randomisation inference 3. Precision – power, and blocked randomisation 4. Ethics – the deception of the people whom an audit studies ::: :::: ::: {.todaytake .fs-85} You leave able to say what random assignment guarantees in this audit, what it leaves open, and what a sharper design would have changed ::: ::: {.todaymeta} Work along in the workspace, in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.) ::: ::: notes Welcome to the third day. Yesterday you worked on the claim as analyst number six: you reproduced a recorded result, declared one analysis and placed it on the curve. Today we go underneath that work, and this first session is about the design of the experiment itself. We start with what random assignment buys and how a reader can check it, and with the names, which carry the treatment and tell their readers more than one thing. Then two questions of analysis: what the comparison among replies can mean, and the test that the design itself supplies. Then precision, where power and blocking lead us to the failed replication. We end on ethics, because an audit deceives the officials whom it studies, and twice along the way you run something in the workspace yourselves. ::: # PART 1 – Random assignment {#part-1-random-assignment .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 1 ::: ::: notes Part one. Everything that the course has said about this claim rests on one sentence of the paper, the sentence that says how the names were assigned. So we start there, with what random assignment guarantees and what it leaves to chance, and with the check of balance that any reader can run on the public file. Then the treatment itself. The officials received a name rather than a group, and a name says more than one thing about the person who signs it. ::: ## Random assignment {#random-assignment .smaller} ::: {.claimcard} "Each housing authority was randomly assigned (via random number generator) to receive an email from one of six different accounts with putatively white, Hispanic, and black names" the original authors (OAs), p. 8 ::: ::: {.small} - The authorities that received Santiago Martinez and those that received Brett Smith differ **only by chance** in everything else: size, community, staffing, how busy the office was that week - A difference in how the two groups of emails were answered is then an **effect of the name**, with chance as the only rival explanation, and a test puts a number on chance - In the causal graph of Task 2 nothing points into the name, which is why `adjustmentSets()` returned the empty set ::: ::: {.src} @EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, accepted manuscript, p. 8. ::: ::: notes This is the sentence on which the whole case rests, and from here on I call its two authors the original authors, or OAs. A random number generator decided which of the six accounts wrote to each authority. So the authorities that received each name are alike in everything except the name, apart from chance: their size, their communities, their staff, how busy they were that week. That is what lets us read a difference in the replies as an effect of the name. It is also why the graph that you finished yesterday has nothing pointing into the name, and why adjustmentSets came back empty. When a machine chose the name, no common cause of the name and the greeting can exist. Chance remains, and chance is what the tests measure. Notice one thing that the sentence does not say: how likely each of the six accounts was to be drawn. ::: ## Balance {#balance .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Share of the emails White names Black names Hispanic names p, chi-square
With a hard-to-find address 45.4% 43.2% 46.7% 0.634
Top third of percent Hispanic 34.4% 33.7% 32.0% 0.505
Top third of percent Black 32.5% 32.2% 35.0% 0.931
Top third of population 36.3% 32.2% 31.7% 0.596
Top third of the poverty rate 31.5% 33.1% 35.0% 0.505
Top third of the HUD assessment 30.3% 34.3% 29.3% 0.672
``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .small} No characteristic comes near a significant difference, as random assignment leads one to expect. The six accounts were not used equally, though: each sent between 145 and 207 emails, a spread that equal chances would rarely produce ($\chi^2$ = 17.1 on 5 df, p = 0.004). Unequal groups cost a little precision, and they bring no bias. ::: ::: {.src} cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv and display_names.csv. The paper reports its own check, without a test, in Table SI1 of the supplemental information (p. 8). ::: ::: notes Random assignment can be checked on anything that the emails could not have changed. The public file holds six such characteristics: whether the address was hard to find, and five characteristics of the community or of the authority, given in thirds. For each I show the share of each group of emails in the top third, and a chi-square test of whether the whole distribution is the same in the three groups. None comes near significance. Read that test for what it is: a check that the assignment was carried out as described. It does not say that a covariate is needed to remove bias, because chance imbalance is exactly what randomisation allows for. [advance] One thing is odd. The six accounts sent between a hundred and forty-five and two hundred and seven emails each, which equal chances would rarely produce. The paper does not say what the chances were. The unequal groups cost some precision and bring no bias, because every authority was still assigned at random. ::: ## Names as treatments {#names-as-treatments .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](housing-experiments_files/figure-revealjs/d3-name-pairs-1.png){width=912} ::: ::: ::: {.small} - A name says more than the group. The OAs matched the ages that the white and Black names suggest, but "virtually all distinctively Hispanic names ... peak in the 1990s and 2000s" (p. 10), so Santiago and Gabriela may also have read as younger - Names meant to indicate one group differ in how often readers perceive them as members of it [@Gaddis2017HowBlackAre] - With two names in each group, the direction agrees and the size differs. Strictly, the experiment estimates the effect of an email signed Santiago or Gabriela Martinez rather than Brett or Emily Smith ::: ::: notes The treatment in a correspondence study is a name, and a name tells its reader more than one thing. The OAs chose their names with care. They matched the ages that the white and the Black names suggest, but they could not match the Hispanic ones, which all peak in popularity in the 1990s and 2000s. So Santiago and Gabriela may have suggested a younger sender as well as a Hispanic one. Gaddis showed the wider problem for names meant to indicate Black applicants: readers do not perceive them all the same way. Two names in each group help. The chart sets the male pair against the female pair. The direction agrees, the size differs, and the intervals overlap widely. Strictly, then, the experiment estimates the effect of an email signed Santiago or Gabriela Martinez, and the step from those names to Hispanic applicants is a question of measurement. The replication kept male names only, chosen from pre-tested ones. ::: # PART 2 – Analysis {#part-2-analysis .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 2 ::: ::: notes Part two takes two questions of analysis that the design raises. The first is the one that the causal graph raised yesterday: the greeting exists only for the emails that drew a reply, and the replies were not assigned at random. We look at what the OAs did about it and at how far the problem could reach. The second is the test that random assignment supplies by itself, without any model of the errors, and the part ends with your first run in the workspace. ::: ## The comparison among replies {#the-comparison-among-replies .smaller} ::: {.small} - A greeting exists only where a reply exists. The names were assigned to the authorities, but **the replies were not assigned at all** - Comparing greetings among replies conditions on a consequence of the name, the collider of yesterday, and mixes an effect on **how** officials write with a difference in **which** officials wrote [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment; @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias] ::: ::: {.fs-75} | Hispanic against white names | Gap (points) | p | Emails | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | Any reply, among delivered emails | −4.8 | 0.214 | 665 | | Greeted by name, among coded replies | −20.0 | 0.0001 | 362 | | Greeted by name, among delivered emails | −13.3 | 0.0001 | 662 | ::: ::: {.fragment .claimcard .fs-75} "As above, we also did this analysis coding all non-responses as unfriendly responses to address the truncation problem. This does not affect the results." the OAs, p. 18, note 11 ::: ::: {.src} cases/housing/data/display_outcomes.csv: differences in proportions with HC2 tests. @EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, accepted manuscript, p. 18. ::: ::: notes You met this problem yesterday as a graph. A greeting exists only where a reply exists. The names were assigned to the authorities at random, but nobody assigned the replies. If a Hispanic name discourages some officials from answering, the officials who answered Santiago need not resemble those who answered Brett, and the gap among replies mixes how officials write with which officials wrote. The table gives the three numbers that matter. Hispanic names drew replies about five points less often, not significantly. Among the coded replies the gap in greetings is twenty points; among every delivered email, thirteen. [advance] The OAs knew all this. Their footnote calls it the truncation problem, and their supporting information truncation by death, a term borrowed from medical statistics. The footnote says that counting every non-response as unfriendly does not affect the results. The footnote is right about the conclusion, although the two numbers answer two different questions, and the next slide asks how far apart they could be. ::: ## A bound on the comparison among replies {#a-bound-on-the-comparison-among-replies .smaller} ::: {.small} - **Assume** that a Hispanic name can only discourage a reply: no official would answer Santiago and ignore the same email from Brett - Then the replies to white names include some from officials who would not have answered a Hispanic name: the extra **7.8%** of the white replies, given by the gap in the rates of coded replies - Take that share out of the white replies in the two most extreme ways: once only replies that greeted by name, once only replies that did not ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Among the officials who would have replied to either name, the gap lies between **−24.9** and **−16.6** points, before any allowance for chance. Even the end nearest zero is a large gap, if the assumption holds, and no data can check the assumption. ```{.r} attrition::estimator_trim(Y = greeted, Z = hisp, R = responded, monotonicity = "treatment_decreases_response", data = delivered) ``` ::: ::: {.src} Trimming bounds from the attrition package, on the 665 delivered emails to Hispanic and white names (cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv); companion/experiments.qmd, section 4. ::: ::: notes How far could a change in who replied go towards explaining the gap among replies? A bound answers that under one assumption, which I want you to hear clearly: a Hispanic name can only discourage a reply, never encourage one. No official answers Santiago and ignores the same email from Brett. Then the replies to white names hold an extra slice, about eight per cent of those replies, from officials who would not have answered a Hispanic name. We do not know which replies make up the slice, so we take the slice out in the two most extreme ways: first assuming that every reply in it greeted by name, then that none did. [advance] Whatever that slice looked like, the gap among the officials who would have replied to either name lies between minus twenty-five and minus seventeen points, so even the near end is a large gap. That conclusion holds only as far as the assumption does, and the data cannot test it. ::: ## Randomisation inference {#randomisation-inference .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](housing-experiments_files/figure-revealjs/d3-ri-hist-1.png){width=912} ::: ::: ::: {.small} - **The sharp null**: the name made no difference to any official, so only the labels could have fallen differently [@Fisher1935DesignExperiments] - The p-value is the share of reshuffles at least as extreme as the observed gap, the observed assignment counted as one of the reshuffles [@PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues] ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Among all delivered emails, a reshuffle repeats the assignment of the design; among the replies, it holds fixed a set that the design never fixed. With 1,999 reshuffles, p = 0.0005 among the replies and 0.0005 among all delivered emails, the smallest possible value. ::: ::: {.src} cases/housing/data/display_ri.csv (4,999 reshuffles among the coded replies) and the column `p_ri` of spec_curve.csv (1,999 reshuffles for each specification). ::: ::: notes Random assignment also supplies a test that needs no model of the errors, and the idea goes back to Fisher. Suppose the name made no difference at all to any official, so that every authority would have answered exactly as it did whichever name arrived. Under that hypothesis, the sharp null, the outcomes are fixed and only the labels could have fallen differently. So we reshuffle the labels, again and again, and recompute the gap each time. The histogram shows what chance alone produces among these replies: ninety-five per cent of the reshuffled gaps lie between minus ten and plus ten, and the observed gap sits far out at minus twenty. [advance] Reshuffling among all delivered emails repeats the design exactly, whereas reshuffling among the replies treats the replies as a fixed set. The sharp null allows that, since a name that changes nothing changes no reply either, but the design never fixed that set, which is the problem of the last two slides again. ::: ## Hands-on 1 – Balance and the reshuffles {#hands-on-1-balance-and-the-reshuffles .smaller} ::: {.small} **In the workspace**, with `index.qmd` open and its setup chunk run: 1. Once, in the console: `pak::pak("ri2")`, which installs randomizr and estimatr with it 2. **Balance.** Tabulate one characteristic by group, then test it, and try another: `datawizard::data_tabulate(audit, select = "poverty_third", by = "group", proportions = "column")` and `chisq.test(table(audit$group, audit$poverty_third))` 3. **Reshuffles among the replies**, on the rows of the reference specification: ```{.r} frame <- spec_frame(audit) # the 362 coded replies to Hispanic and white names set.seed(20261106) reshuffled <- ri2::conduct_ri(y ~ hisp, assignment = "hisp", sharp_hypothesis = 0, declaration = randomizr::declare_ra(N = nrow(frame), m = sum(frame$hisp)), data = frame, sims = 1999) summary(reshuffled) ``` 4. Run the same on `spec_frame(audit, population = "all")`. **Which of the two reshuffles repeats the assignment of the design?** ::: ::: notes Your turn. Open the report in your IDE and run its setup chunk, which reads the data and loads the helpers. Install ri2 once; it brings the two packages that it needs, randomizr and estimatr. First, balance: tabulate one characteristic by group with data underscore tabulate, then run the chi-square test, and try a second characteristic of your choice. Then the reshuffles. Spec underscore frame, one of the helpers, returns the rows of any specification of the curve, and with no arguments it gives the reference: the coded replies to Hispanic and white names. Conduct underscore ri reshuffles the names among those rows nineteen hundred and ninety-nine times, as the experiment assigned the names, and summary gives the share of reshuffles at least as extreme. Then do the same among every delivered email, and write one sentence on which of the two repeats the design. [state the time] STUCK in chat if you need me. ::: # PART 3 – Precision {#part-3-precision .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 3 ::: ::: notes Part three is about precision: how large a gap a design of this size can find, and what a different way of assigning the names would have bought. Both questions lead to the replication, which emailed three times as many authorities and assigned its names within each state. You met the power of the two designs briefly yesterday. Here we read the same curves more closely, and then look at blocking, which the replication used and the original did not. ::: ## Power {#power .smaller} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](housing-experiments_files/figure-revealjs/d3-power-1.png){width=912} ::: ::: ::: {.small} - Power depends on the size of the gap, on the number of replies and, for a 0/1 outcome, on the share itself, whose variance is $p(1 - p)$ - The original comparison reaches a power of 0.8 only for a gap of 14.6 points, and an estimate has to exceed about 10.2 points to be significant at 5% - The replication planned its first round to achieve "90% power to detect 75% of the original effect size" ::: ::: {.src} cases/housing/data/display_power.csv, from `power.prop.test()`; the preregistration of the replication, osf.io/2ug8x. ::: ::: notes Power is the probability that a study of a given size detects a gap of a given size. It depends on three things: the gap, the number of observations, and how variable the outcome is, which for a zero-or-one outcome follows from the share itself. The dashed line marks a power of zero point eight, the usual target when a study is planned. With about a hundred and eighty replies a group, the original comparison reaches it only for a gap of nearly fifteen points; the replication reaches it at ten. And in the original comparison an estimate has to exceed about ten points before it is significant at all. The replication planned its first round to detect three quarters of the original effect with a power of ninety per cent. What a significant estimate from a design of the original size says about the size of the gap is the subject of the third session today. ::: ## Blocked randomisation {#blocked-randomisation .smaller} :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="54%"} ::: {.small} - **The original audit** drew a name for each authority, without blocks - **The replication**: "We will block randomize within each U.S. state to ensure that there is an equivalent number of Hispanic and white names contacting the housing agencies within each state" - Blocking assigns the names at random **within groups formed before the experiment**, in fixed numbers, so the groups of names are balanced on the blocking variable by design, not only in expectation - It buys **precision**, as far as the blocking variable predicts the outcome, and it **removes no bias**, since random assignment has already removed it [@ImaiEtAl2008MisunderstandingsExperimentalistsObservationalists; @AtheyImbens2017EconometricsRandomizedExperiments] ::: ::: ::: {.column width="46%"} ::: {.small} **The original, analysed within the two kinds of address** ::: ::: {.fs-75} | Analysis | Gap | SE | |:--|--:|--:| | Ignoring the address | −19.97 | 5.165 | | Within the two kinds | −19.95 | 5.159 | ::: ::: {.fragment .small .fs-85} Chance had already balanced the two kinds: 51.6% and 51.8% of the replies from each kind came to Hispanic names. A blocked design would have guaranteed that balance, and narrowed the spread of the reshuffled gaps only from 5.33 to 5.24 points. ::: ::: :::: ::: {.src} The preregistration of the replication, osf.io/2ug8x; the reference comparison with estimatr and ri2 (cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv); companion/experiments.qmd, section 7. ::: ::: notes The original audit drew one name for each authority, with nothing grouped beforehand. The replication blocked: within each state it assigned equal numbers of Hispanic and white names. Blocking means forming groups on something recorded before the experiment and randomising within each group in fixed numbers, so that the groups of names are balanced on it by design rather than only in expectation. What it buys is precision, and only as much as the blocking variable predicts the outcome. It removes no bias, because random assignment has already removed it. [advance] The original can show what blocking on the address would have changed. The address does predict the greeting: white names were greeted by name in two thirds of the replies to easy addresses and just over half of the others. Yet the gap and its standard error barely move, because chance had already given the two kinds of address the same share of Hispanic names, so the guarantee of a blocked design would have been worth little here. ::: ## Hands-on 2 – Power and blocks {#hands-on-2-power-and-blocks .smaller} ::: {.small} **In the workspace**, with `frame` from Hands-on 1: 1. **Power.** `power.prop.test(n = 181, p1 = 0.61, p2 = 0.51)` gives the power of the original comparison for a gap of 10 points below a white share of 61%. Then set `n = 369`, the replies of a group in the replication 2. Change `p2` until the power of the original comparison reaches 0.8. **Which gap is that, and how does it compare with the published 20 points?** 3. **Blocks.** `estimatr::difference_in_means(y ~ hisp, data = frame)`, then the same with `blocks = hard_email`. **What changes, and why so little?** ::: ::: {.fragment .small} For your notes: one sentence on what a replication with 369 replies a group could find that the original could not. ::: ::: notes Your turn again. Power dot prop dot test is base R, and it gives the power of a test of two proportions: with a hundred and eighty-one replies a group, a white share of sixty-one per cent and a Hispanic share of fifty-one, a gap of ten points, you should find a power just under one half. Then set n to three hundred and sixty-nine, the replies of a group in the replication. Next, change p2 until the power of the original comparison reaches zero point eight, and compare that gap with the published twenty points. Then the blocks. Difference in means from estimatr, first without blocks and then with the hard-to-find address as the blocks, and look at the standard error. [state the time] [advance] Before we move on, one sentence for your notes: what could a replication with three hundred and sixty-nine replies a group find that the original could not? ::: # PART 4 – Ethics {#part-4-ethics .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"} ::: {.partlabel} Part 4 ::: ::: notes The last part is short, and it is not a technical one. An audit study deceives the people whom it studies, and its data describe officials who never agreed to take part. The OAs devote a section of their paper to these costs, and the replication had to weigh them again. We read what the OAs wrote, then what the public file does to protect the officials, and we end with a question for you about replication itself. ::: ## Deception {#deception .smaller} ::: {.small} The officials who answered Santiago Martinez spent working time on a request from someone who did not exist, and never learned that their reply was data. The OAs set out their reasons in the paper: ::: ::: {.small} - They "contacted government employees in their professional capacity" - The emails were "not designed to alter their behavior but rather to measure it" - They were "attentive to minimizing the amount of time workers devoted to requests for information from fictitious constituents", and did not write again, even when a reply asked a question - "This deception is necessary to experimentally test whether bureaucrats exhibit racial biases in their responses to constituents" ::: ::: {.src} @EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, accepted manuscript, pp. 11–12. ::: ::: notes Every official who answered Santiago Martinez spent working time on someone who did not exist, and never learned that the reply had become data. The OAs take this seriously, in a section of its own. They wrote to public employees in their professional capacity. The emails were meant to measure behaviour, not to change it. They kept the request short, so that a link or a pasted paragraph would answer it, and they never wrote back, even when an official asked a question in return. And they argue that the deception is necessary: without random assignment of the names there is no way to measure whether officials answer people differently by race or ethnicity. Whether you find that argument sufficient is a judgement that research ethics committees make for every audit, and one that you may one day have to make yourselves. ::: ## The officials in the data {#the-officials-in-the-data .smaller} ::: {.small} - The public file gives the size, poverty and ethnic composition of each community only in thirds, because "Whether or not a housing official responded, particularly to an ostensible minority applicant, is very sensitive and potentially harmful information" (the ReadMe of the OAs) - The replication kept the rule: "Due to Institutional Review Board restrictions, the publicly available dataset will include only the tercile version of the demographic covariates to minimize likelihood of identifying subjects" (its final report) - The course works only with the blinded file and never tries to recover an authority ::: ::: {.fragment .small} Replication has a cost of its own in this kind of research: the SCORE replication sent **3,050** further requests from people who did not exist to offices of the same kind. ::: ::: {.src} The ReadMe of the replication package, doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU; the final report of the replication, osf.io/2ug8x. ::: ::: notes The second cost concerns the data. Whether an official replied to an ostensibly minority applicant is sensitive information about a real person in a real office, and the OAs say so in the ReadMe of their package. That is why the public file gives the communities only in thirds: the exact census values would identify the authorities, and with them the officials. The replication followed the same rule under its own review board. It is also why the course never tries to recover an authority from the file, and why nothing that we do needs to. [advance] And replication has a cost of its own here. To test the claim again, SCORE sent three thousand and fifty further fictitious requests to offices of the same kind, so a decision to replicate an audit weighs that burden on the officials against what a second answer is worth. ::: ## Replicating an audit {#replicating-an-audit .questionslide} ::: {.none} The replication found no gap in greetings by name. Would a third audit of housing authorities be worth its cost to the officials, and what would its design have to change to justify that cost? ::: ::: notes So here is a question for the class, and there is no answer on the next slide. The replication found no gap. Would a third audit of housing authorities be worth its cost to the officials who would answer it, and what would its design have to change to justify that cost? Draw on what this session has covered: the names, the comparison among replies, the power of each design, the blocks. Talk to your neighbour first, then I will take a few answers. [state the time; take three or four answers, and ask each speaker which part of the design their answer would change] ::: ## The reading and the next session {#the-reading-and-the-next-session .smaller} ::: {.small .nonincremental} - **The reading**: [Audit experiments](../companion/experiments.html), the module of the companion curriculum behind this session, with the code of each analysis and a task that reverses the assumption of the bound - **Next**: Binary outcomes. The greeting as a 0/1 outcome, the difference in proportions as a regression with HC2 standard errors, logistic regression, odds ratios against average marginal effects, and why a covariate changes an odds ratio even in an experiment ::: ::: notes That is the design. The module Audit experiments, in the companion curriculum on the site, is the reading for this session: it has the code behind the analyses of this session, and a task that turns the assumption of the bound around, which is a good test of whether the idea has stuck. The next session stays with the same comparison but changes the question. Instead of asking how the names were assigned, it asks how a zero-or-one outcome is modelled: as a difference in proportions, as a linear regression with the standard errors that the course uses, and as the logistic regression of the paper, with its odds ratios. ::: ## References {.scrollable .smaller visibility="uncounted"} ::: {#refs} :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
